subject: Creative Arts
source: NaCCA Creative Arts Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4–6 (September 2019)
accessibility: Read prompts and choices aloud when needed. Practical responses may use classroom materials, movement, speech or drawing.

indicators.statement: Study some visual artworks created by Ghanaian and other African visual artists living in Africa and examine how the artworks reflect the history and culture of the people in Africa.
indicators.content_standard: B5.1.1.1 Generate ideas for artistic expression from people, culture, environment and topical issues.

skills.description: Identify the subject, artistic method and evidence in a work.
Study and describe in visual arts.
Use artistic evidence to explain a choice or improvement.

questions.stem: After studying El Anatsui's use of joined bottle tops, pupils link paper shapes printed with images of traded goods. What is this work about?
options: Goods passing between communities
A waterway shaping life in a city
Repairing cloth to reduce waste
Trees and traders sharing a street
questions.answer: Goods passing between communities
hints: Identify the action or subject at the centre.
questions.explanation: The described action centres on goods passing between communities.

questions.stem: After studying El Anatsui's use of joined bottle tops, pupils link paper shapes printed with images of traded goods. Which detail could a learner point out in the work?
options: A stitched patch beside a worn section
Tree shapes overlapping the roofs of stalls
A row of dark boats along a pale curve
Linked pieces bearing pictures of goods
questions.answer: Linked pieces bearing pictures of goods
hints: Look for a detail the example actually describes.
questions.explanation: The evidence in the example is linked pieces bearing pictures of goods.

questions.stem: After studying El Anatsui's use of joined bottle tops, pupils link paper shapes printed with images of traded goods. Which method is used?
options: Joining small units into a hanging
Layering silhouettes on a folding map
Placing contrasting scenes side by side
Stitching and arranging fabric samples
questions.answer: Joining small units into a hanging
hints: Think about how the parts were made or performed.
questions.explanation: The example uses joining small units into a hanging to show goods passing between communities.

questions.stem: A pot has a wide mouth and two handles. What might its handles help a person do?
options: Close its mouth
Change its colour
Lift the pot
Make it deeper
questions.answer: Lift the pot
hints: Look at the way hands could hold it.
questions.explanation: Look at the way hands could hold it. Lift the pot.

questions.stem: A rough rock and a smooth bottle appear in a drawing. What is the artist showing by changing the marks on their surfaces?
options: The price
Texture
The title
The date
questions.answer: Texture
hints: Imagine how each surface would feel.
questions.explanation: Imagine how each surface would feel. Texture.

questions.stem: After studying El Anatsui's use of joined bottle tops, pupils link paper shapes printed with images of traded goods. Which idea does the work suggest?
options: Trees give shade to people working outdoors
Trade connects the places goods pass through
Crossings link neighbourhoods divided by water
Repair can extend the life of cloth
questions.answer: Trade connects the places goods pass through
hints: Connect the detail to the idea it expresses.
questions.explanation: The detail of linked pieces bearing pictures of goods supports the idea that trade connects the places goods pass through.

questions.stem: After studying El Anatsui's use of joined bottle tops, pupils link paper shapes printed with images of traded goods. Which source would help the class check its account?
options: A tailor explaining a repair in the town studied
A museum account of El Anatsui's materials and methods
A partner school's photograph of a refill station
A labelled street study from the African city shown
questions.answer: A museum account of El Anatsui's materials and methods
hints: Choose evidence about the actual subject.
questions.explanation: The closest source for this subject is a museum account of El Anatsui's materials and methods.

questions.stem: After studying El Anatsui's use of joined bottle tops, pupils link paper shapes printed with images of traded goods. Which sentence describes evidence before giving an opinion?
options: The work will win first prize.
Everybody will like the finished piece.
Linked pieces bearing pictures of goods.
The maker must have found the work easy.
questions.answer: Linked pieces bearing pictures of goods.
hints: Choose a detail you can check in the example.
questions.explanation: Linked pieces bearing pictures of goods. This detail can be checked without guessing what someone thinks.

questions.stem: Which words describe a pattern you can see on cloth?
options: Triangles repeat along the edge.
The cloth must be very old.
Everyone likes the cloth.
The maker was in a hurry.
questions.answer: Triangles repeat along the edge.
hints: Describe what the eye can check.
questions.explanation: Describe what the eye can check. Triangles repeat along the edge.

questions.stem: Two prints have the same subject. One is made with bold blocks, the other with thin lines. What differs?
options: The fact that both are prints
The number of subjects studied
The place named in both titles
The way the subject is shown
questions.answer: The way the subject is shown
hints: Look at how the marks are made.
questions.explanation: Look at how the marks are made. The way the subject is shown.

questions.stem: A learner says one example shows how everyone in a country lives. Which reply fits the evidence?
options: The biggest artwork always speaks for all communities.
Every artist in that country must share that one view.
A work made long ago shows exactly how everyone lives today.
It shows one view. Other communities may show different experiences.
questions.answer: It shows one view. Other communities may show different experiences.
hints: Consider how many people's experiences one example can represent.
questions.explanation: Consider how many people's experiences one example can represent. It shows one view. Other communities may show different experiences.

questions.stem: Two people remember a festival differently. How could you learn more before making a picture or a play about it?
options: Pick the story with the most characters
Ask what each person saw and compare their accounts
Put the two dates together as one date
Choose the story told in the loudest voice
questions.answer: Ask what each person saw and compare their accounts
hints: Think about what each person actually witnessed.
questions.explanation: Think about what each person actually witnessed. Ask what each person saw and compare their accounts.

questions.stem: After studying El Anatsui's use of joined bottle tops, pupils link paper shapes printed with images of traded goods. Which change would make the main detail easier to recognise?
options: Use a contrasting stitch around the patch
Leave parts of the stalls visible under the tree shapes
Repeat a goods symbol across one join to link two sections
Make the stopped arrows visible beside the waste
questions.answer: Repeat a goods symbol across one join to link two sections
hints: Keep the aim and strengthen the clue the audience needs.
questions.explanation: This change helps the audience notice linked pieces bearing pictures of goods.

questions.stem: A class uses linked paper pieces after studying El Anatsui. Which comment explains an artistic connection?
options: The class adapted the method of joining small units to tell its own story.
Using the same number of pieces proves the meaning is identical.
Paper and metal must produce identical surfaces.
Giving both works the same price makes them related.
questions.answer: The class adapted the method of joining small units to tell its own story.
hints: Look for a shared method and a different artistic decision.
questions.explanation: Look for a shared method and a different artistic decision. The class adapted the method of joining small units to tell its own story.

questions.stem: After studying El Anatsui's use of joined bottle tops, pupils link paper shapes printed with images of traded goods. A partner wants to know why the artist chose this method. Which reply explains the choice?
options: It guarantees that everyone will have the same feeling.
It proves this is the only way to make the piece.
It shows the artist used the most costly tools.
It helps show goods passing between communities.
questions.answer: It helps show goods passing between communities.
hints: Ask what this choice helps the audience notice.
questions.explanation: Joining small units into a hanging helps communicate the subject through linked pieces bearing pictures of goods.

questions.stem: A picture shows a market long ago. Which detail could help you learn about work there?
options: The tools in the sellers' hands
The number of corners on its label
The day you visited the picture
The colour of the museum door
questions.answer: The tools in the sellers' hands
hints: Find evidence inside the picture.
questions.explanation: Find evidence inside the picture. The tools in the sellers' hands.

questions.stem: A visitor says a work feels joyful. What would turn this feeling into an explanation?
options: Write the price next to the title
Count the visitors who came in that day
Repeat the word joyful more loudly
Point to a feature that gives that impression
questions.answer: Point to a feature that gives that impression
hints: Connect a feeling to something in the work.
questions.explanation: Connect a feeling to something in the work. Point to a feature that gives that impression.

questions.stem: A child says a painted clay bowl is both useful and decorative. Why?
options: Painting makes the bowl deeper.
It must cost twice as much.
It can hold things and its painted marks can be enjoyed.
All bowls have the same marks.
questions.answer: It can hold things and its painted marks can be enjoyed.
hints: Think about what the bowl does and how it looks.
questions.explanation: Think about what the bowl does and how it looks. It can hold things and its painted marks can be enjoyed.

questions.stem: You want to learn what has changed over time. Which pair would help most?
options: Two copies of the same photograph
An older example and a recent one from the same community
Two guesses about the maker's name
Two labels for the same display shelf
questions.answer: An older example and a recent one from the same community
hints: Look for evidence from two times.
questions.explanation: Look for evidence from two times. An older example and a recent one from the same community.

questions.stem: After studying El Anatsui's use of joined bottle tops, pupils link paper shapes printed with images of traded goods. What do you notice about goods passing between communities? Describe one detail in the example and explain what it tells you about life in a community in Africa.
hints: Connect the detail to the idea it expresses.
questions.explanation: For example, connect linked pieces bearing pictures of goods to the idea that trade connects the places goods pass through. Other supported choices are welcome.

criteria.description: Identifies the subject in the example.
Describes a detail and links it to the subject or setting.

options: Linked pieces bearing pictures of goods
Arrows stopping at a pile of waste
Tree shapes overlapping the roofs of stalls
A stitched patch beside a worn section
questions.answer: Linked pieces bearing pictures of goods
hints: Look for a detail the example actually describes.
questions.explanation: The evidence in the example is linked pieces bearing pictures of goods.

questions.stem: After studying El Anatsui's use of joined bottle tops, pupils link paper shapes printed with images of traded goods. Which technique could a pupil borrow for a new idea?

Joining small units into a hanging
Stitching and arranging fabric samples
Placing contrasting scenes side by side

questions.stem: You want a new border based on waves. Which drawing develops the idea?
options: A label with the date of the visit
A row of curved marks that rise and fall
An unrelated list of boat names
A square left empty beside the page
questions.answer: A row of curved marks that rise and fall
hints: Find a visual feature of waves that can repeat.
questions.explanation: Find a visual feature of waves that can repeat. A row of curved marks that rise and fall.

questions.stem: A learner has drawn an idea for a round container. What else should the learner draw to help plan it?
options: A price without a drawing
The name of an unrelated song
A second signature
A side view showing its depth
questions.answer: A side view showing its depth
hints: A flat view may hide the container's form.
questions.explanation: A flat view may hide the container's form. A side view showing its depth.

questions.stem: After studying El Anatsui's use of joined bottle tops, pupils link paper shapes printed with images of traded goods. Which idea could still be shared in a different version?
options: Trade connects the places goods pass through
Bottles can be filled again here
Trees give shade to people working outdoors
Repair can extend the life of cloth
questions.answer: Trade connects the places goods pass through
hints: Connect the detail to the idea it expresses.
questions.explanation: The detail of linked pieces bearing pictures of goods supports the idea that trade connects the places goods pass through.

questions.stem: After studying El Anatsui's use of joined bottle tops, pupils link paper shapes printed with images of traded goods. Which source could help a pupil develop the subject further?

A tailor explaining a repair in the town studied
A museum account of El Anatsui's materials and methods
A labelled street study from the African city shown

hints: Choose evidence about the actual subject.
questions.explanation: The closest source for this subject is a museum account of El Anatsui's materials and methods.

questions.explanation: Linked pieces bearing pictures of goods. This detail can be checked without guessing what someone thinks.

questions.stem: You like the woven lines on a basket. Which idea uses that observation in a new design?
options: Draw crossing bands on a paper bookmark
Use the maker's name as your own
Trace the whole basket label
Copy the price from the shelf
questions.answer: Draw crossing bands on a paper bookmark
hints: Borrow a visible feature for a different use.
questions.explanation: Borrow a visible feature for a different use. Draw crossing bands on a paper bookmark.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to show that one figure is important. Which sketch is worth trying?
options: Give that figure more space than the others
Make every part equally hard to see
Hide that figure behind the frame
Draw only the title and leave out all figures
questions.answer: Give that figure more space than the others
hints: Think about what attracts the eye.
questions.explanation: Think about what attracts the eye. Give that figure more space than the others.

questions.stem: What should a group keep in a record of its ideas?
options: Only the final mark and no examples
Early versions and a note about why one was chosen
Only the names of pupils who finished first
A list of every chair in the hall
questions.answer: Early versions and a note about why one was chosen
hints: Keep enough to follow how the idea changed.
questions.explanation: Keep enough to follow how the idea changed. Early versions and a note about why one was chosen.

questions.stem: You have three ideas on separate cards. Two seem to tell parts of one story. What could you try?
options: Choose a fourth idea without reading the cards
Place them together and skip checking the result
Remove both because they are similar
Combine the two and check whether the story still makes sense
questions.answer: Combine the two and check whether the story still makes sense
hints: Check what the combination communicates.
questions.explanation: Check what the combination communicates. Combine the two and check whether the story still makes sense.

questions.stem: After studying El Anatsui's use of joined bottle tops, pupils link paper shapes printed with images of traded goods. Which suggestion develops the existing idea?

Leave parts of the stalls visible under the tree shapes
Repeat a goods symbol across one join to link two sections
Turn some boat shapes towards the landing
questions.answer: Repeat a goods symbol across one join to link two sections
hints: Keep the aim and strengthen the clue the audience needs.
questions.explanation: This change helps the audience notice linked pieces bearing pictures of goods.

questions.explanation: Look for a shared method and a different artistic decision. The class adapted the method of joining small units to tell its own story.

options: It guarantees that everyone will have the same feeling.
It shows the artist used the most costly tools.
It helps show goods passing between communities.
It proves this is the only way to make the piece.
questions.answer: It helps show goods passing between communities.
hints: Ask what this choice helps the audience notice.
questions.explanation: Joining small units into a hanging helps communicate the subject through linked pieces bearing pictures of goods.

questions.stem: Two tiny sketches show different views of a stall. Why look at both?
options: To avoid choosing a viewpoint
To decide which sheet has the neatest back
To decide which view shows the action better
To count who sharpened a pencil first
questions.answer: To decide which view shows the action better
hints: A change in viewpoint can reveal a detail.
questions.explanation: A change in viewpoint can reveal a detail. To decide which view shows the action better.

questions.stem: You cannot visit the place you want to study. What could still help you develop an idea?
options: Copy a friend's guess as a first-hand account
Choose a random place and call it the same one
Leave the place out and keep its name as the title
Use labelled pictures or recordings from that place
questions.answer: Use labelled pictures or recordings from that place
hints: Use evidence that identifies the place.
questions.explanation: Use evidence that identifies the place. Use labelled pictures or recordings from that place.

questions.stem: Which choice develops a symbol for sharing?
options: Copy a picture of an empty wall
Draw the border first and leave the subject undecided
Write a different date at every corner
Try two hands passing one bowl between them
questions.answer: Try two hands passing one bowl between them
hints: Use a visible action to express the idea.
questions.explanation: Use a visible action to express the idea. Try two hands passing one bowl between them.

questions.stem: Which question helps turn an observation into a plan?
options: How could I show the part that caught my attention?
Which design has the largest price tag?
How many pupils are in the next class?
Where is my name in the register?
questions.answer: How could I show the part that caught my attention?
hints: Turn a detail you noticed into an artistic choice.
questions.explanation: Turn a detail you noticed into an artistic choice. How could I show the part that caught my attention?.

questions.stem: After studying El Anatsui's use of joined bottle tops, pupils link paper shapes printed with images of traded goods. Use the example to invent two ideas for a visual artwork about goods passing between communities. Show one idea and say how it differs from the example.
hints: Connect the detail to the idea it expresses.
questions.explanation: For example, connect linked pieces bearing pictures of goods to the idea that trade connects the places goods pass through. Other supported choices are welcome.

criteria.description: Offers two ideas connected to the subject.
Develops and explains an original idea from the example.

How far is the hall from the road?
What day will the class go home?
How did you put the parts of the work together?

It proves every home has that same object.
It means the object is the artist's favourite.
It tells us the exact date of every event.
questions.answer: It can show an activity people know well.
hints: Look for a link between the object and how people live.
questions.explanation: Look for a link between the object and how people live. It can show an activity people know well.

It is the best. It is better than the rest.

The frame is brown.
The drawing has a title.
The figures are small beside it.

hints: Compare the sizes within the picture.
questions.explanation: Compare the sizes within the picture. The figures are small beside it.

Change the title and treat it as the class's work
Ask whether the speaker agrees to that use
Share a shortened version without asking
